concepts.title: Why Do We Need a Parliament?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Why Do We Need a Parliament?' refers to.
questions.a: A legislature concentrates the people's representatives in one chamber where laws are debated, governments are questioned and public grievances get a hearing. It institutionalises disagreement: instead of settling conflicts in the street, a democracy argues them out on the floor of the house and decides by voting.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Why Do We Need a Parliament?'.
questions.a: Parliament is the debating floor of the nation -- where conflict becomes law through argument and vote.

concepts.title: Two Houses of Parliament: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Two Houses of Parliament: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha' refers to.
questions.a: India's Parliament has two chambers. The Lok Sabha is directly elected for five years and holds the purse and confidence powers. The Rajya Sabha represents the states, with members elected indirectly by state legislatures for six-year staggered terms; it can delay and revise ordinary legislation and alone can authorise Parliament to legislate on state subjects.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Two Houses of Parliament: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha'.
questions.a: One house answers to the people now; the other guards the states and continuity -- bicameralism balances both.

concepts.title: Powers of Parliament: Law-Making and Control over Executive

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Powers of Parliament: Law-Making and Control over Executive' refers to.
questions.a: Parliament legislates on union and concurrent lists and, under special conditions, state subjects; it alone sanctions taxation and spending through the budget. Its control weapons include question hour, zero hour, censure and no-confidence motions, adjournment motions, and standing committees that scrutinise ministry working in detail.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Powers of Parliament: Law-Making and Control over Executive'.
questions.a: Purse, laws and question time -- parliament's levers over government run from budgets to no-confidence.

concepts.title: Declining Effectiveness of Parliament: Debates and Debates

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Declining Effectiveness of Parliament: Debates and Debates' refers to.
questions.a: Critics note a gap between Parliament's design and its practice: declining deliberation, disruptions, anti-defection squeezing individual MPs' judgement, and the executive's dominance over the calendar and business. Defenders answer that committees still work, and accountability survives through scrutiny and elections -- the debate over parliamentary effectiveness remains open.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Declining Effectiveness of Parliament: Debates and Debates'.
questions.a: Designed as the master, often reduced to a rubber stamp -- the health of parliament decides the health of democracy.
